PREFACE.
Tur Publishers of the “ Provincial Wesleyan Almanack’’ cannot
omit the opportunity (in publishing the second volume) of thanking the
public for the very cordial reception given te their publication of last
year. The most encouraging testimonials, have been received from
every quarter approving their labors,—a most gratifying proof of which
was found in the rapid sale of this Annual last year—the whole edition
being exhausted in two months from first date of issue.
A discerning public will perccive in every page of the present volume
the evidences of thought and labor, with a laudable anxiety to secure
general approbation.
The arrangement of the different departments will be found much
more complete—a great deal of new matter, not hitherto found in such
| a publication, has been introduced. Every portion has been most
carefully revised up to the date of publication. The “ Balifax Business

Directory ” is still continued, with the latest known alterations; while
nothing has been knowingly omitted which could secure this annual
volume being all that is required for the Merchant, the Mariner, the Far-
mer, and the Family. oe

| care visible in its varied departments to render it attractive and uscful
| —will secure for this and succeeding numbers a very rapid and exten

Cause OF THE AURORA-BOREALIS.—M, de la i ve, the celebrated |
ing French Astronomer, explains the production of the Aurora-Borealis in |
the following .manner:—“ When the sun, having passed into the |
Southern hemisphere, no longer heats*so much of our hemisphere, |
the aqueous vapors which have accumulated during the summer | 3
in this part of *the atmosphere begin to condense, the kind of| as
humid cap enveloping the polar regions extends more and more, | a
and facilitates the passage of the electricity accumulated in the stat
y 24 upper portions of the air. But in these elevated regions, and |
vi especially at this period of the year, the aqueous vapors must fre- |
27 s } quently pass into the state of minute pariicles of ice or snow floating |
be 3 in the air, similar to these which give rise to the halos; they form, as |
7 it were, a kind of semi-transparent mist. These half-frozen fogs |
20 conduct the electricity to the surface of the earth, near the pole, and |
94 are at the same time illumined by these currents or electric discharges. |
In fact-all observers agree in asserting that the Aurora-Barealis is.
constantly preceded by a mist, which rises from the pole, and the |
margins of which, less dense than the remainder, are colored the first; |
and indeed it is very frequent near the pole in the winter months, and |
especially in those where there is abundance of vapor in the air.

To Miuk Cows.—A cow should be milked clean. Nota drop, if 1t can be avoid- |
ed, should be left in the udder. It has been proved that the half-pint that comes |
out dast has twelve times, I think it is, as much butter in it as the half-pint that |
comes out first. The udder would seem to be a sort of milk pan, in which the |
cream is uppermost, and, of course, comes out last, seeing that the outlet is at the |
bottom. But, besides this, if you do not milk clean, the cow will give less and
less milk, and will become dry much sooner than she ought.— Cobbett. |
x Raisina Peuttry.—There is scarcely any branch of farming operations more
productive than the raising of poultry for market; and yet with a large ma- |
jority of our agriculturalists, it is considered of but little account. The proximity |
toa great market, and the facilities for reaching it possessed by many of our.

MANURE For CLover.—Some farmers make it a rule to spread about fifty bushels
per acre of ashes over their clover in March, which they flud, from long experience
to be a good manure for this grass. Wood-ashes will be useful on any soil; coal-
ashes Chiefly on stiff clays. On the stiff soils of sume parts of Buckinghamshire,
ashes of all kinds are*much esteemed, and have risen to a high price.
ImPoRTANT Fact 1n AGRICULTURE.—Whatever may be the nature of tho soil, or
of the crop cultivated, it should always be the aim of the farmer to grow full
crops. Partial and somewhat extensive failures will even then but too often occur;
but to neglect making the best known preparations, or only to prepare for half a
crop, has a direct tendency to unprofitable farming.
How To PresrravE Manurz.—Put it in heaps, and cover it over with earth two
feet deep. Never leave manure in the barn yard; put it all, year by year, on your
land.

To Improve THB Woo or SHREP by SHEARING.—Immediately after the sheep |
aro shorn soak the roots of the wool that remain all over with oil, or butter |
and brimstone; and three cr four days afterwards wash them with salt and
| water. The wool of the next season will not only be much finer, but the quan- |
tity will be in much greter abundance. It may be depended upon that the |
sheep Will not be troubled with scab or vermin that year. Salt water is a safe and |
etfectual remedy against maggots.
To Preserve CATTLE FROM DISEASE IN THE WinTER.—When cattle are kept
out in the winter it is recommended as a useful practice to rub some tar at the
root of the horn, which prevents the wet from getting between the root and the |
skin, and, it is said, contributes to preserve the health of the animal and to keep
it from the various diseases to which it may otherwise be liable.

| inches diagonal, which comes into a cupboard set into a wall, but with its end 80
| near the bottom that there hall never be above a desirable quantity in the cup-

| the oats are kept constantly sweet (the taking away one gallon moving the whole
above), which, when laid up otherwise in great quantities, frequently grow |
musty.

PACKETS FROM HALIFAX.
The Steamer for England arrives from the United States at Cunard’s
wharf fortnightly, that is about midnight every other Thursday, and the
same week the Ste: mer from, Engfand arrives and proceeds to Boston,
Messrs. Cunard & Co. have also Steam Packets running to Bermuda
and St. John’s, N. F.,—the latter touches at Sydney.
The Steamer astern State leaves Brown’s wharf every other Tucs-
day for Boston, and touches at Yarmouth on the way. Messrs. Young
& Hart have two packets running continually to Boston, viz: the
barque Halifar, and the brig Boston; the latter is commanded by
Capt. O’Brien, and the former by Capt. McCullough.
A packet runs between Halifax and Liverpool, Queen’s Co., leaving
Cronan’s Wharf occasionally through the month.
Two fine schooners—the Sylvia and the Lunenburg Packet—sail about
| every ten days for Lunenburg,—the former from Black’s, and the latter
from Oxley’s wharf,
The Guysborough Pac ket sails fiom the Long Wh if.
